analysis.investment_thesis: Dilip Buildcon trades near book value (P/B 0.98) and below 15x trailing earnings, which superficially satisfies two Graham filters, but the debt/equity of 1.71 and interest coverage of roughly 1.7x make this a highly leveraged speculation, not a sound investment. Losses in FY2022 (-₹550 Cr) and FY2023 (-₹1 Cr) break the required streak of consecutive positive earnings, and persistently negative free cash flow signals that stated profits are not translating into real owner cash.
key_strengths: P/B of 0.98 trades at a slight discount to book value — the one genuine Grahamian comfort here
Trailing P/E of 11.4 is below the 15x ceiling, and revenue has compounded at 11.6% over nine years
Operating cash flow was positive all five years (₹44–₹2,845 Cr range), showing the business does generate gross operating cash
key_risks: Debt/equity of 1.71 vastly exceeds my 0.5 ceiling; borrowings surged from ₹7,240 Cr to ₹10,375 Cr in a single year (FY2025)
Interest coverage ≈ 1.7x (Operating Income ₹2,159 Cr ÷ Finance Costs ₹1,249 Cr) — well below the 3.5x minimum I require

Earnings are unreliable: two loss years in the last five, a forward P/E of 26.9 vs. trailing 11.4 implies the market expects a sharp profit decline, and ₹417 Cr of 'Other Income' props up FY2025's ₹840 Cr net profit
red_flags: Free cash flow is negative every single year (-₹4,134 Cr in FY2025) — profits are an accounting construct here, not cash in the owner's pocket
Net losses in FY2022 and FY2023 destroy the 5-year consecutive positive earnings test that is non-negotiable in my framework
Debt resurged sharply in FY2025 after deleveraging (FY2023 borrowings ₹6,658 Cr → FY2025 ₹10,375 Cr), signalling the balance sheet is structurally dependent on rolling credit
No dividend history mentioned — a company with this debt load has nothing left for shareholders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Dilip Buildcon passes only the most superficial of my quantitative screens. The Graham Number — √(22.5 × EPS ₹51.7 × BVPS ₹355) ≈ ₹643 — sits above the current price of ₹457, which would normally interest me. However, the Graham Number is predicated on stable, reliable earnings and a clean balance sheet. Neither condition is met. With debt/equity at 1.71, net borrowings of ₹10,375 Cr against equity of ₹5,772 Cr, and finance costs consuming ₹1,249 Cr against operating income of ₹2,159 Cr, the company is one bad contract cycle or rising interest rate environment away from repeating FY2022's ₹550 Cr loss. A margin of safety cannot exist when the company's solvency depends on continuous refinancing.

The cash flow picture is equally disqualifying. Free cash flow has been negative in every reported year, reaching -₹4,134 Cr in FY2025 with capex of ₹4,265 Cr. In my experience, an enterprise whose book of infrastructure contracts demands perpetual external financing is not a business generating owner earnings — it is a machine that converts shareholder equity and bank credit into fixed assets for the government. The forward P/E of 26.9 versus trailing 11.4 tells me that analysts expect the ₹840 Cr FY2025 profit — itself heavily assisted by ₹417 Cr of Other Income — to be unsustainable. For the disciplined investor, there is insufficient margin of safety at any price when the debt burden, earnings volatility, and cash burn are this severe.
